rationale.Chest X-ray: Not required, but would be abnormal. May show anterior mediastinal mass.
rationale.CT chest with contrast / MRI chest: CT chest is essential to rule out thymoma, seen in 10-15% of MG patients. Thymoma appears as anterior mediastinal mass.
rationale.CBC with differential: Good screening tool in nearly every patient.
rationale.ECG, 12 lead: Generalized weakness can be cardiac. ECG rules out cardiac etiologies.
rationale.Pulse oximetry: Oxygenation is lower than usual — likely from hypoventilation due to respiratory muscle weakness.
rationale.Sedimentation rate, erythrocyte: Not required but would be abnormal in autoimmune disease.
rationale.HCG, beta (pregnancy test): All female patients of childbearing age should have pregnancy test before imaging and treatment.
rationale.TSH, serum: Hypothyroidism is associated with generalized weakness — important to screen.
rationale.Acetylcholine receptor antibody, serum: Positive detection strongly supports MG diagnosis. ~80% positive in generalized MG.
rationale.Electromyography: EMG with repetitive stimulation shows decremental response — decreased signal with each stimulation. Differentiates from Lambert-Eaton (which shows incremental response).
rationale.Tensilon test: Not required but would be positive in MG. Edrophonium temporarily improves muscle strength.
rationale.PT/PTT / INR: Patient is likely to have surgery (thymectomy) — pre-surgical labs needed.
rationale.Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive: BMPs are excellent screening tools in any differential.
rationale.Methylprednisolone / Prednisone / Azathi: Corticosteroids and azathioprine are first-line immunosuppressive treatments for MG.
rationale.Pyridostigmine / Neostigmine: Pyridostigmine is for symptomatic treatment only — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases ACh at neuromuscular junction. Does NOT treat underlying disease. Use in conjunction with immunosuppressants.
rationale.Consult surgery / Thymectomy: Thymoma should be surgically removed. Thymectomy can lead to complete remission in ~85% of patients without further medication.
rationale.IVIG: [Auto-split from bundled label "IVIG / Plasmapheresis"] Can be used pre-thymectomy for severe symptoms. However, expensive — conservative trial of steroids + pyridostigmine first is reasonable if patient is stable.
rationale.Plasmapheresis: [Auto-split from bundled label "IVIG / Plasmapheresis"] Can be used pre-thymectomy for severe symptoms. However, expensive — conservative trial of steroids + pyridostigmine first is reasonable if patient is stable.
rationale.Instruct patient, smoking cessation: One of the most important things for health — address smoking.
rationale.Advise patient, safe sex techniques: Patient has history of STIs — review safe sex practices.
rationale.Reassure patient: New chronic diagnosis causes anxiety — reassure and inform.
rationale.Papanicolaou smear: HPV DNA test every 3 years for women ≥30. No history given — should be scheduled.
rationale.Tdap vaccine: Tdap every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.
rationale.Intubation / mechanical ventilation (too: Patient has respiratory muscle weakness but intubation is invasive and can often be avoided with medical management of MG first.
rationale.Pyridostigmine as monotherapy: Pyridostigmine only treats symptoms. In a patient with respiratory involvement, immunosuppression (steroids/azathioprine) is needed to treat the underlying autoimmune process. Pyridostigmine also increases airway secretions.

hpi: {{patient_name}} is a woman of childbearing age who presents with progressive generalized weakness that worsens with continued muscle use and improves with rest. She has developed ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Respiratory muscle involvement is present with mild hypoxemia from hypoventilation. Exam reveals fatigable weakness with preservation of sensation and reflexes — the hallmark of myasthenia gravis. The underlying pathophysiology is autoimmune antibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. CT chest is essential to evaluate for thymoma, which is present in 10-15% of MG patients and whose resection can lead to remission in ~85%.

physical_exam: Generalized fatigable weakness. Worsens with continued use, improves with rest.
Hypoventilation from respiratory muscle weakness. Decreased oxygen saturation. Monitor for myasthenic crisis.

Ptosis (eyelid drooping). Dysarthria. Dysphagia. Proximal asymmetric limb weakness. Fatigable weakness — repeat muscle testing worsens performance. Sensation and reflexes preserved. Differentiates from Lambert-Eaton and neuropathy.
Mild ptosis. Facial muscle weakness may affect chewing and speech.

case_summary: Myasthenia gravis with thymoma. Autoimmune antibodies against AChR → fatigable weakness. CT chest shows anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma, ~15% of MG). Treatment: steroids + pyridostigmine + thymectomy. Avoid pyridostigmine monotherapy in respiratory involvement.
